notes.text: A season — A certain time appointed by God for its being and continuance, which no human wit or providence can alter. And by virtue of this appointment of God, all vicissitudes which happen in the world, whether comforts or calamities, come to pass. Which is here added to prove the principal proposition, That all things below are vain, and happiness is not to be found in them, because of their great uncertainty, and mutability, and transitoriness, and because they are so much out of the reach and power of men, and wholly in the disposal of God. Purpose - Not only natural, but even the voluntary actions of men, are ordered and disposed by God. But it must be considered, that he does not here speak of a time allowed by God, wherein all the following things may lawfully be done, but only of a time fixed by God, in which they are actually done.
To die — And as there is a time to die, so there is a time to rise again, a set time when they that lie in the grave shall be remembered.
To kill — When men die a violent death. To heal - When he who seemed to be mortally wounded is healed.
To weep — When men have just occasion for weeping.
Stones — Which were brought together in order to the building of a wall or house. To embrace - When persons perform all friendly offices one to another.

To life — When men lose their estates, either by God's providence, or by their own choice. To cast away - When a man casts away his goods voluntarily, as in a storm, to save his life, or out of love and obedience to God.
To rent — When men rend their garments, as they did in great and sudden griefs.
To love — When God stirs up love, or gives occasion for the exercise of it.

What profit — Seeing then all events are out of man's power, and no man can do or enjoy any thing at his pleasure, but only when God pleaseth, as has been shewed in many particulars, and is as true and certain in all others, hence it follows, that all men's labours, without God's blessing, are unprofitable, and utterly insufficient to make them happy.

Seen — I have diligently observed mens various employments, and the different successes of them. Hath given - Which God hath imposed upon men as their duty; to which therefore men ought quickly to submit. Exercised - That hereby they might have constant matter of exercise for their diligence, and patience, and submission to God's will and providence.

He hath — This seems to be added as at apology for God's providence, notwithstanding all the contrary events and confusions which are in the world. He hath made (or doth make or do, by his providence in the government of the world) every thing (which he doth either immediately, or by the ministry of men, or other creatures) beautiful (convenient, so that, all things considered, it could not have been done better) in its time or station, (when it was most fit to be done). Many events seem to mens shallow judgments, to be very irregular and unbecoming, as when wicked men prosper, and good men are oppressed; but when men shall throughly understand God's works, and the whole frame and contexture of them, and see the end of them, they will say, all things were done wisely. He hath set - It is true, God hath put the world into mens hearts, or made them capable of observing all the dispensations of God in the world; but this is to be understood with a limitation, because there are some more mysterious works of God, which no man can fully, understand, because he cannot search them out from the beginning to the end.
Them — In creatures or worldly enjoyments. To do good - To employ them in acts of charity and liberality.
Should eat — Use what God hath given him.

glossa.text: *All things have their time.* ((HIER.)) Above he taught the uncertain and fluctuating state of the human condition, etc., *as far as* they are contained neither by place nor by time.
*A time to plant,* etc. ((ID.)) It is doubtful to none, etc., *as far as* because perfect charity casteth out fear.

*A time to destroy,* etc. We cannot build up good things, unless we have first destroyed the evil ones, as it was said to Jeremias by God, that he should first root up and dig under and destroy, and afterwards build and plant ((Jerem. I)).

*A time to mourn,* etc. We must mourn now, that in the time to come we may dance that dance which David [danced] before the ark of the testament ((II Reg. VI)). Displeasing to the daughter of Saul, he pleased God the more.

*A time to scatter stones,* etc. ((HIER.)) I wonder, etc., *as far as* and calls to penance.

*A time to embrace.* A time to embrace wisdom, and to cleave more strictly to contemplation; and a time to be made far from the embrace, namely of wisdom, that we may serve the care of the time, and those things without which we cannot live.

*A time to keep silence, and a time.* ((HIER.)) We teach in the churches what we do not know. We do not learn any of the arts without a teacher, this alone is so cheap and so easy that it does not need a master. Nothing seems to us to be right, save what we learn, so that after much silence we may be made masters out of disciples.

 *A time to speak.* The discipline of Pythagoras is to keep silence for five years, and afterwards, being learned, to speak.

*A time of love.* A time of loving, after God, wives, children, kinsfolk, and a time of hating them, in martyrdom. Or, *Because now we see through a glass in a dark manner ((I Cor. XIII))*, etc. There will be a time of loving the presence of God, and a time of hating, when, beholding face to face and advancing unto better things, we shall begin to hate and to despise what we have loved.

*A time of war.* Now, for those not doing penance; a time of peace in the time to come, when all Israel shall be saved; *A time of war,* be not secure, take the armour of God.
*I have seen the affliction which he gave,* etc. ((HIER.)) It is said that God therefore, etc., *as far as* he made them to grow, to remain and to be changed even to the end of the age.
*And I have known.* ((HIERON.)) Therefore man was set as a husbandman in the world, etc., *as far as* hence:

*Every man that eateth and drinketh,* etc., For many now are the tribulations of the just, but in the time to come there shall be no labour in Jacob.

*I have learned,* etc. ((ID.)) There is nothing new in the world, the course of the sun, the changes of the moon, the dryness of the earth and of the trees, or their greenness, were founded together with the world; and these things God therefore tempered by a fixed reckoning, that we might understand the Providence of God in them, and might fear before the face of God. But the countenance of the Lord is upon them that do evil things.

notes.text: In — Not only in Israel, but among all nations. Which shews that this psalm speaks of the Messiah, and the times of the New Testament. Heavens - Where thy throne of glory is established, where the blessed angels celebrate thy praises, where Christ sitteth at thy right hand in glorious majesty, from whence he poureth down excellent gifts upon babes.

Babes — Weak and foolish, and contemptible persons, who are frequently called babes or children. Such are very unfit to grapple with an enemy: and therefore when such persons conquer the most powerful and malicious enemies, it must needs confound them, and advance the glory of God: as indeed it did, when such mean persons as the apostles, and disciples of Christ, maintained and propagated the gospel, in spite of all the wit, power, and rage of their enemies. Ordained - Perfectly or firmly settled strength; that is, the praise of his strength or power, Matt. xxi, 16, it is rendered praise. Still - Silence and confound them. Avenger - The devil, and all who are his vassals and espouse his quarrel.

The moon — Either the sun is included under this general title: or he omitted it, because he made this psalm by night. Ordained - Placed in that excellent and unalterable order, and directed to their several motions.

What is man — How mean and inconsiderable a thing is man, if compared with thy glorious majesty. Man - Hebrew. infirm, or miserable man. By which it is apparent that he speaks of man, not according to the state of his creation, but as fallen into a state of sin and misery, and mortality. Mindful - Carest for him, and conferest such high favours upon him. The son - Hebrew. the son of Adam, that great apostate from God, the sinful son of a sinful father, his son by likeness of disposition and manners, no less than by procreation. All which tends to magnify the following mercy. Visitest - Not in anger, as that word is sometimes used, but with thy grace and mercy.

For — Thou hast in Christ mercifully restored man to his primitive estate, wherein he was but one remove below the angels; from which he was fallen by sin. Crowned - Man, fallen and lost man: who is actually restored to glory and dominion in Christ his head and representative, who received this crown and dominion for man's good, and in his stead; which he will in due time communicate to his members. And so the two expositions of this place concerning mankind and concerning Christ, may be reconciled. For he speaks of that honourable estate conferred first upon Christ, and then by his hands upon mankind. But the words more literally rendered are, Thou madest him a little less than God. And hence some have inferred, that man in his original state was the highest of all creatures. David praises God for giving him victory over his enemies, ver. 1-6. Triumphs in confidence that God would judge the world and protect his people, ver. 7-10. Calls others to praise him, ver. 11, 12. Prays for help, and praises God, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician upon Muth-labben, A psalm of David Title of the psalm. Muth-labben - This also seems to be a title of some tune, or instrument: of which we may be content to be ignorant, as the Jewish doctors are.

glossa.text: « O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name! etc. » ((CASS.)) First the praises of God, his majesty, and his exalted working are described. « In the whole. » ((Ibid.)) Let not the Jews therefore, or any others, claim for themselves what belongs to all, which is the intent. « Above the heavens. » ((AUG.)) Literally, or the Scriptures: because it exceeds the utterances of all the Scriptures; or, « above the heavens. » Continuing with what follows, that is, into the Scriptures, which he bends down to babes, on account of the enemies of the cross: who are destroyed, when the Scriptures are seen, that is, understood, to be led down as far as babes: and when through them they are nourished unto strength, and are raised to the sublimity of understanding.

« Out of the mouth of infants. » ((Ibid.)) Of the unwise, to whom the Apostle gave milk, whom those signified who praised the Lord, in whom the Lord uses this testimony. Out of these he hath perfected praise, because if only the perfect were in the Church, no counsel would be taken for the human race; as now, when even the least, not yet capable of the knowledge of spiritual things, are nourished by faith in the history of things temporal. « Enemies » are all who speak things contrary to the dispensation made through the Crucified. « Defenders » the heretics seem of the faith, the philosophers of wisdom, although yet the former impugn the faith, and the latter true wisdom. « Sucklings, » ((CASS.)) not in age, but as Peter has it, « as newborn babes ((I Petr. II)), » who cannot yet take food, but milk; and it is: thou art proclaimed not only by the perfect, but also by the unwise. Or, he calls infants and sucklings the apostles, who were simple and unlearned men; whence: « The foolish things of the world « God hath chosen, that he may confound the strong ((I Cor. I)). » The praise is more perfect. Or, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, that is, out of the words of the Hebrew children thou hast perfected praise, which seemed to be done childishly, on account of the enemies, that it might not seem to be human wisdom, but divinely given. « Thine enemies. » The pagans. « The enemy. » The Jew, who is an enemy of God, while he defends the Father alone: because « he that honoureth not the Son, honoureth not « the Father, » or an enemy in his will.

« For I shall see. » Before the Jew, in spirit. « Thy heavens, » the apostles, I shall see present in their descendants; this well suits those of the first age. « The works of thy fingers. » Because they are perfected by the cooperation of the Trinity, which is signified here in the three fingers, as there: « Who weigheth the bulk of the earth with three fingers. » ((Isa. XL.)) And through them, « The moon and the stars which thou hast founded. » Not they.

« What is man. » ((Ibid.)) Secondly, he says that the nature of man, once corrupted, is exalted in Christ above all things. For before he had shown the omnipotence of the Godhead. By man, sinners; by the son of man, the spiritual. ((Ibid.)) Man, any vile person, of whom God is mindful in showing mercy, the Son of man, Christ as man: since through him thou visitest him, when the Word was made flesh, in which the physician came to the sick. « Or the son. » ((AUG.)) The disjunction hints that there is a distance between man and the son of man. Every son of man is man, but not conversely, as Adam. Every man therefore, who bears the image of the earthly: the Son of man, who is heavenly, and deservedly a new man, son of man: because the new is made out of the old by a certain change. ((AUG.)) Why, leaving the higher things, does he speak of these lowest ones? But the sheep, etc., *as far as* who by the seed of the word of God make the hearts of men to bear fruit.

« Moreover the cattle also. » He notes therefore that the wicked also are subject to Christ, which seems less: for these carnal men dwell in the breadth of the plain, that is, in the amplitude of pleasures, not in the mountains of virtues. « The cattle of the field. » ((Ibid.)) Who live in the flesh, where they climb nothing steep: but the broad way, to which they cling, is that which leads to destruction: whence also Abel is slain in the field.

« The birds, » the proud: of whom, « They have set their mouth against heaven ((Psal. LXXII)). » Whose head says: « I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High ((Isa. XIV)). « The fishes of the sea that walk through the paths of the sea, » the curious. These three, the pleasure of the flesh, pride, curiosity, include all vices, which are the concupiscence of the flesh, the ambition of the world, that is, pride, the concupiscence of the eyes, since through the eyes curiosity chiefly prevails.

notes.text: And I saw — So it runs, chap. xix, 11, xx, 1, 4, 11, in a succession. All these several representations follow one another in order: so the vision reaches into eternity. A new heaven and a new earth - After the resurrection and general judgment. St. John is not now describing a flourishing state of the church, but a new and eternal state of all things. For the first heaven and the first earth - Not only the lowest part of heaven, not only the solar system, but the whole ethereal heaven, with all its host, whether of planets or fixed stars, Isai xxxiv, 4 Matt. xxiv, 29. All the former things will be done away, that all may become new, verses 4, 5, 2 Pet. iii, 10, 12. Are passed away - But in the fourth verse it is said, "are gone away." There the stronger word is used; for death, mourning, and sorrow go away all together: the former heaven and earth only pass away, giving place to the new heaven and the new earth.

And I saw the holy city — The new heaven, the new earth, and the new Jerusalem, are closely connected. This city is wholly new, belonging not to this world, not to the millennium, but to eternity. This appears from the series of the vision, the magnificence of the description, and the opposition of this city to the second death, chap. xx, 11, 12; xxi, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9; xxii, 5. Coming down - In the very act of descending.
They shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God — So shall the covenant between God and his people be executed in the most glorious manner.

And death shall be no more — This is a full proof that this whole description belongs not to time, but eternity. Neither shall sorrow, or crying, or pain, be any more: for the former things are gone away - Under the former heaven, and upon the former earth, there was death and sorrow, crying and pain; all which occasioned many tears: but now pain and sorrow are fled away, and the saints have everlasting life and joy.

And he that sat upon the throne said — Not to St. John only. From the first mention of "him that sat upon the throne," chap. iv, 2, this is the first speech which is expressly ascribed to him. And he - The angel. Saith to me Write - As follows. These sayings are faithful and true - This includes all that went before. The apostle seems again to have ceased writing, being overcome with ecstasy at the voice of him that spake.

And he — That sat upon the throne. Said to me, It is done - All that the prophets had spoken; all that was spoken, chap. iv, 1. We read this expression twice in this prophecy: first, chap. xvi, 17, at the fulfilling of the wrath of God; and here, at the making all things new. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end - The latter explains the former: the Everlasting. I will give to him that thirsteth - The Lamb saith the same, chap. xxii, 17.

glossa.text: *And I saw.* In this seventh vision he treats of the renewing of the elements and the glorification of the saints, describing the merits through which the saints are thus glorified. *A new heaven and a new earth.* The change of the air and of the earth is not doubtful, but that it comes to pass through fire. But concerning water there is doubt, for it is believed to have purgation in itself.

*As a bride adorned.* As a bridegroom sends gifts beforehand to his bride before he leads her home, so does Christ send to the Church faith and virtues and good works before he receives her into glory.

*A great voice from the throne.* When he had said that he had seen the renewing of the elements and the glorification of the saints, this was unknown, and, lest it should seem past believing, he adds the authority of the holy Fathers, who foretold this. *Behold the tabernacle.* That is, it is plain that the humanity of Christ shall be in that same glory in which it warred, and the men who imitated him and used those things well.

 *And they his people.* That is, offending in nothing, which cannot be while they are in mortal flesh.
*And death.* Truly there shall be no tears there, because there shall be no cause of tears.

*And he said.* As if he should say: Write whatsoever has been shown thee concerning this renewing. This was done for the profit of those now present, for whom I have been bidden to write these things. *Write: for these,* etc. Bidding him write, and announce to others, he subjoins an exhortation, that all may labour to belong to this renewing.

*And he said to me.* When the authority of the saints concerning this renewing has been set down, he sets down the authority of God himself. *It is done.* Lest anyone should ask: What shall come to pass after that renewing, it is said to him that nothing remains to be done.

 *Alpha and Omega.* As if he should say: This renewing I shall be able to make, because I created all things, and in me all things shall be consummated. *To him that thirsteth.* I will give, not to him that thirsteth for an hour, but to him that perseveres.

notes.text: Inherit the kingdom — Purchased by my blood, for all who have believed in me with the faith which wrought by love. Prepared for you - On purpose for you. May it not be probably inferred from hence, that man was not created merely to fill up the places of the fallen angels?

I was hungry, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink — All these works of outward mercy suppose faith and love, and must needs he accompanied with works of spiritual mercy. But works of this kind the Judge could not mention in the same manner. He could not say, I was in error, and ye recalled me to the truth; I was in sin, and ye brought me to repentance. In prison - Prisoners need to be visited above all others, as they are commonly solitary and forsaken by the rest of the world.

Then shall the righteous answer — It cannot be, that either the righteous or the wicked should answer in these very words. What we learn herefrom is, that neither of them have the same estimation of their own works as the Judge hath.
Inasmuch as ye did it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye did it to me — What encouragement is here to assist the household of faith? But let us likewise remember to do good to all men.
Depart into the everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels — Not originally for you: you are intruders into everlasting fire.
Then will they answer — So the endeavour to justify themselves, will remain with the wicked even to that day!

And these shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life everlasting — Either therefore the punishment is strictly eternal, or the reward is not: the very same expression being applied to the former as to the latter. The Judge will speak first to the righteous, in the audience of the wicked. The wicked shall then go away into everlasting fire, in the view of the righteous. Thus the damned shall see nothing of the everlasting life; but the just will see the punishment of the ungodly. It is not only particularly observable here

1. That the punishment lasts as long as the reward; but,

2. That this punishment is so far from ceasing at the end of the world, that it does not begin till then.

glossa.text: *And when.* Being about to be delivered to the cross very soon, he set before them the glory of him who triumphs, that he might make up by this promise for the scandals that were to follow. After the parables about the end of the world, the Lord now sets forth the manner of the judgment to come.

*The sheep from,* etc. There shall be two orders in the judgment, namely of the elect and of the reprobate: but of the elect some shall judge, to whom it is said: *You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the tribes of Israel.* Others shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry and you gave me to eat.* Likewise of the reprobate, some who are outside the Church shall not be judged: others who shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry, and you gave me not to eat,* etc.
*The goats.* The he-goat is a butting and rank-smelling animal, which was offered for sins in the law, and it signifies sinners: nor does he say she-goats, which can have young.

*Blessed of the Father.* Advanced by the benefit of my Father to the obtaining of glory, in which you may reign without corruption, to which you have been predestined from the foundation of the world.

*Then shall they answer.* Not distrusting the words of the Lord, but either amazed at the greatness of the king's majesty; or because every good thing that they did seems little to them, whence it is said: *The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come ((Rom. VIII))*, etc.
*Of these brethren.* My brethren and my mother are they who do the will of my Father.
*You gave me not,* etc. What does he deserve who has seized what belongs to another, if he is eternally damned who has not given anything of his own?

*Lord, when,* etc. They busy themselves to excuse themselves, as though they who were deceiving men could deceive God. But they have no excuse who would not be converted from evils and do alms; whence he adds: *As long as you did it not to one,* etc.

*Into everlasting punishment.* In vain therefore does Origen promise deliverance after many years to evil men and to the demons themselves. *Into everlasting punishment. ((AUG.))* In which matter Origen was assuredly the more merciful, who believed that the devil himself too and his angels, after punishments heavier according to their deserts and of longer duration, were to be rescued out of those torments and joined to the holy angels. But the Church has not undeservedly condemned him, both for this and for sundry other things, and chiefly for the blessednesses and miseries alternating without ceasing, and for the endless goings and returnings from those to these at fixed intervals of ages.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: Verbal and thematic core: 'new heavens and a new earth' (LXX ouranos kainos kai ge kaine) with the 'former things not remembered/passed away' motif — John's 'new heaven and a new earth' and 'the first things have passed away' (v.4) draws on both halves. Strongest availability and recurrence; Hays' volume and thematic coherence both high.

echoes.text: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.
echoes.note: Doublet of 65:17: 'the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me' — reinforces the eschatological permanence theme. Together with 65:17 establishes the dominant intertext.

echoes.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
echoes.note: 'He will wipe away every tear' (v.4) echoes 'the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces' and 'he will swallow up death forever' — joint source for tear-wiping and death's abolition. MT 'swallow up death' vs LXX 'death prevailed having swallowed' diverges; John follows the death-abolished sense (cf. MT / Theodotion). High volume.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: Covenant-dwelling formula: 'My dwelling place (LXX kataskenosis) will be with them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people' — directly behind v.3 ('God's dwelling is with people... they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God'). Recurrence with Lev 26 strengthens.

echoes.text: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: Foundational covenant formula: 'I will set my tabernacle/dwelling among you... I will walk among you and be your God, and you shall be my people.' Source of the Ezek 37:27 reuse; Revelation's plural 'peoples' (laoi, best text) universalizes the singular covenant 'people.'

echoes.text: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion; for, behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst,’ says Yahweh. Many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you.
echoes.note: 'I will dwell in the midst of you... and many nations shall join themselves to the LORD... and shall be my people' — supports v.3's expanded 'peoples' and the God-dwelling-with-humanity theme; verbal contact with the dwelling formula.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.
echoes.note: 'Awake, awake... O Jerusalem, the holy city; put on your beautiful garments' — behind the 'holy city' title (v.2) and the adornment imagery; recurs at 21:27 ('nothing unclean shall enter').

echoes.text: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
echoes.note: Bridal-adornment simile (v.2): 'as a bridegroom decks himself... and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels' — close conceptual and verbal match for 'prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.'

echoes.text: For Zion’s sake will I not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteousness go out as brightness, and her salvation as a lamp that burns. The nations shall see your righteousness, and all kings your glory, and you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of Yahweh shall name. You shall also be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. You shall no more be termed Forsaken; […]
echoes.note: Zion as bride married to God: 'as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride... so shall your God rejoice over you'; the city given a new name. Supports the New Jerusalem-as-bride identification.

echoes.text: The Yahweh’s ransomed ones will return, and come with singing to Zion; and everlasting joy will be on their heads. They will obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.”
echoes.note: 'Sorrow and sighing shall flee away' parallels 'no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain' (v.4); paired with 51:11. Thematic coherence high though verbal contact diffuse.

echoes.text: The ransomed of Yahweh shall return, and come with singing to Zion; and everlasting joy shall be on their heads. They shall obtain gladness and joy. Sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
echoes.note: Doublet of 35:10 ('sorrow and sighing shall flee away'); reinforces the abolition-of-grief catalogue in v.4.

echoes.text: and I will bring them, and they will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and they will be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.”
echoes.note: 'They shall be my people and I will be their God' — another instance of the covenant formula feeding v.3; faint given many parallel attestations.

echoes.text: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”
echoes.note: 'I will say... You are my people, and they shall say, You are my God' — covenant-formula reuse; low independent weight beside Lev 26 / Ezek 37.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The 'peoples' (laoi) who serve in the everlasting kingdom may color the plural in v.3; faint and contested.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'New heaven and a new earth' as deliberate recreation of the Gen 1 'heavens and the earth' — figural new-creation framing; structurally cued but verbally generic.

echoes.text: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old.
echoes.note: 'Remember not the former things' — paired with 43:19 (next pericope); supports 'the first/former things have passed away' (v.4).

echoes.text: Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?
echoes.note: 'Am I the sea?' / the sea as chaos-monster domain may underlie 'the sea is no more' (v.1); part of the OT chaos-sea / Leviathan complex.

echoes.text: Daniel spoke and said, I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the sky broke out on the great sea. Four great animals came up from the sea, diverse one from another.
echoes.note: The 'great sea' from which the beasts arise — 'the sea is no more' (v.1) as the elimination of the source of chaos/the beast (cf. Rev 13:1). Figural; contested.

echoes.text: Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
echoes.note: 'Behold, I am making all things new' (v.5) draws on 'Behold, I am doing a new thing' (idou ego poio kaina, LXX) — the 'behold... new' formula. High verbal contact with the LXX of Isa 43:19.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
echoes.note: 'I will give freely (dorean) to him who is thirsty from the spring of the water of life' (v.6) echoes 'Ho, every one who thirsts, come to the waters... without money' — free gift to the thirsty. Verbal ('thirsty,' 'freely/without price') and thematic match.

echoes.text: This is what Yahweh, the King of Israel, and his Redeemer, Yahweh of Armies, says: “I am the first, and I am the last; and besides me there is no God.
echoes.note: 'I am the first, and I am the last' underlies 'the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End' (v.6); recurs at Rev 1:8,17; 22:13. Cf. also Isa 41:4; 48:12 for the same self-predication.

echoes.text: I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son' — Davidic adoption formula directly behind 'I will be his God, and he will be my son' (v.7). Revelation democratizes the royal promise to every overcomer.

echoes.text: He will call to me, ‘You are my Father, my God, and the rock of my salvation!’ I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.
echoes.note: Davidic sonship: 'He shall cry to me, You are my Father, my God... I will make him the firstborn' — reinforces 2 Sam 7:14 behind v.7; royal-firstborn coloring.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel my called: I am he; I am the first, I also am the last.
echoes.note: 'I am the first, I also am the last' — doublet of 44:6 supporting the Alpha-Omega self-designation (v.6).

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that living waters will go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter will it be.
echoes.note: 'Living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem' supports 'the spring of the water of life' (v.6); fully developed in Rev 22:1. Thematic coherence high.

echoes.text: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.
echoes.note: 'With you is the fountain of life' — direct verbal source for 'the spring of the water of life' (v.6); pege zoes in LXX.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.
echoes.note: 'Fire and sulfur (brimstone)' raining on Sodom (v.8 'fire and sulfur') — the canonical brimstone-judgment image. Cf. Ezek 38:22; Ps 11:6.

echoes.text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
echoes.note: 'The fountain of living waters' (God) contrasted with broken cisterns — colors the 'spring of the water of life' (v.6).

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: 'Springs of water will guide them' for the redeemed who 'will not hunger or thirst' — feeds the thirst/spring motif (v.6); also echoed in Rev 7:16-17.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: 'Everyone whose name is written in the book' — undergirds the overcomer/inheritance contrast with the excluded (v.7-8) and the book-of-life of v.27.

echoes.text: With pestilence and with blood will I enter into judgment with him; and I will rain on him, and on his hordes, and on the many peoples who are with him, an overflowing shower, and great hailstones, fire, and sulfur.
echoes.note: 'Fire and sulfur' rained in judgment on Gog — reinforces the 'lake that burns with fire and sulfur' (v.8).

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The Son of Man coming in glory and seated on his throne, before whom all nations/peoples are gathered to serve him, is the direct backbone of v.31-32. Daniel's 'one like a son of man' receives dominion, glory, and kingdom over all peoples, nations, and languages; Matthew transposes this enthronement into the scene of universal judgment.

echoes.text: As for you, O my flock, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.
echoes.note: 'I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats' is the explicit verbal and conceptual source for 'he will separate them... as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats' (v.32-33). The shepherd-judge distinguishing the flock animals is unmistakable.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh to them: Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad; therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: The LORD 'will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep,' saving the weak from those who shove with side and shoulder. This grounds the criterion of judgment on treatment of the vulnerable and the shepherd-king's vindication of the mistreated, mirrored in care for the hungry, naked, sick, and imprisoned.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.
echoes.note: The promise of one shepherd, 'my servant David,' set over the flock as prince, is typologically fulfilled in the Son of Man / King who shepherds and judges the nations. The Davidic shepherd-king of Ezekiel 34 is the figure Matthew casts Jesus as embodying.

echoes.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: The acts of true fasting/righteousness — 'share your bread with the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house, when you see the naked, cover him' — closely match the King's catalog of hungry/stranger/naked in v.35-36. Isaiah 58 is the strongest verbal parallel for the works that mark the righteous.

echoes.text: I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and I will execute judgment on them there for my people, and for my heritage, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations. They have divided my land,
echoes.note: 'I will gather all the nations... and I will enter into judgment with them there' supplies the assize of the nations gathered before the throne (v.32), where they are judged on how they treated God's people.

echoes.text: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there will I sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
echoes.note: 'Let the nations be roused and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.' The enthroned divine Judge seated to judge the assembled nations directly parallels the Son of Man sitting on the throne of his glory to judge all the nations.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.' This supplies the retinue of v.31, 'the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him,' for the day of the LORD's appearing.

echoes.text: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece; if I have lifted up my hand […]
echoes.note: Job's oath of innocence — feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, caring for the needy ('if I have not given the poor their portion... if I have seen any perish for lack of clothing') — supplies a near-checklist of the deeds of mercy that define the sheep.

echoes.text: and if you draw out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul: then your light shall rise in darkness, and your obscurity be as the noonday;
echoes.note: 'If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness' reinforces the same Isaian ethic of self-giving to the afflicted as the substance of righteousness rewarded by God.

echoes.text: and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;
echoes.note: The righteous man 'gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment' — Ezekiel's catalog of the deeds that mark the just from the wicked closely parallels the King's criteria and reinforces the Ezekielian frame already operative in the sheep/goats image.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' This is the precise theology of v.40 — kindness to the least is rendered to the King himself, who repays. The identification of the needy with the divine creditor is the conceptual hinge.

echoes.text: He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.' The principle that treatment of the poor is treatment of God himself underwrites 'you did it to me' / 'you did not do it to me.'

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' This two-fold eternal destiny is the source for v.46, 'these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.'

echoes.text: Also to the poor man stretch out your hand, That your blessing may be perfected. A gift has grace in the sight of every man living; And for a dead man keep not back grace. Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn. Be not slow to visit a sick man; For by such things you will gain love.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's exhortation to stretch out your hand to the poor, give to the needy, not neglect those who weep, and visit the sick supplies a deuterocanonical catalog of mercy-deeds strikingly close to the King's list (feed, clothe, visit the sick).

echoes.text: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots shall be like the whirlwind; to render his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will Yahweh execute judgment, and by his sword, on all flesh; and the slain of Yahweh shall be many.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will come with fire... by fire will the LORD enter into judgment with all flesh' faintly underlies the 'eternal fire' prepared for the cursed and the universal judgment of all flesh/nations.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The closing image of the unquenched fire / undying worm for the rebellious provides scriptural background for the 'eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment' of v.41, 46.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The enthronement of the messianic Lord at God's right hand, with subjugation of enemies, underlies the royal session of the Son of Man on the throne of his glory and the placing of subjects at the right and left.

echoes.text: For he will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper. He will have pity on the poor and needy. He will save the souls of the needy. He will redeem their soul from oppression and violence. Their blood will be precious in his sight.
echoes.note: The royal psalm's portrait of the king who delivers the needy, the poor, and those who have no helper, redeeming their life from oppression, supplies the ideal of the just king whose rule is measured by care for the vulnerable — the standard the King applies.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines. He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, […]
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet on the mountain for all peoples, where death is swallowed up, faintly informs the inheritance/eternal-life reward into which the blessed are welcomed when all nations are gathered.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical promise that the righteous are in God's hand, will be vindicated at the visitation, judge nations, and receive a kingdom/crown, parallels the righteous inheriting the kingdom and the eternal-life reward at the eschatological assize.

echoes.text: In the days of Enemessar, I did many alms deeds to my kindred: I gave my bread to the hungry, and my garments to the naked. If I saw any of my race dead, and cast forth on the wall of Ninevah, I buried him.
echoes.note: Tobit's acts of charity — giving bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and burying the dead — model the very deeds of mercy that mark the righteous and were understood in Second Temple piety as righteousness stored up before God.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's instruction to give alms from your possessions, for almsgiving 'is a good gift in the sight of the Most High' and lays up treasure against the day of necessity, reflects the same logic that deeds to the least are rendered to God and rewarded eschatologically.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds' / the scattering and gathering language of Zechariah faintly resonates with the gathering of all nations before the throne, though the dominant gathering source is Joel 3.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (v.34) presupposes the creation account as the temporal anchor — the kingdom planned since the world's founding, a protological framing of the inheritance.

registers.label: Spare
lines: For everything there is a season under heaven.
A time to be born, and a time to die.
The One on the throne says: I make all things new.
I am the beginning and the end.
Whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.
Lord, when did we see you? Teach us to see.
Come, let us worship at the turning of the year.
Glory to God in the highest! Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: The old year closes and a new one opens, and the One seated on the throne says: See, I am making all things new.
Glory to God in the highest!
For everything there is a season — a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance.
Glory to God in the highest!
He will wipe every tear from our eyes; death and mourning and crying will be no more, for the old order has passed away.
Glory to God in the highest!
So we step into the new year looking for his face in the least of these, and we worship the Alpha and the Omega.
Glory to God in the highest! Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: For everything there is a season under heaven.
Glory to God in the highest!
Behold, says the Lord, I make all things new.
Glory to God in the highest!
He wipes every tear; the old has passed away.
Glory to God in the highest!
Come, let us worship the beginning and the end.
Glory to God in the highest! Amen.
